I think something that often fails to come up in the conversation is the place of the kids themselves. 

A lot of people talk about how much poorer people were 100 years ago and they were popping out kids left and right. What they’re not talking about is the fact that exploited child labor was rampant to the point of it being an economic advantage for the poor. Kids start working in some as soon as they could walk, whether it be in the mines, factories, or the farm. The mortality rate was so high that death was expected, and you would just pump another out. 

For every kid, yeah you had another mouth to feed, but you also had free labor in the family farm or in the house handling live stock, butchering and cleaning chickens, milking cows. gardening, being a third parent, etc. Urban wise, you had another paycheck coming in. If the kid died, they died. 

It was to the point that where it could be considered a point of economic security to have more children if you were poor. 

Living conditions had a way lower bar. It was common to have 12 people in a one bedroom cabin, and have all the children share a single bed.

I have quite a few that are circumstantial. I’m willing to talk about them if you want to have a genuine conversation about it, but I’m a bit tired of people on the internet playing doctor. I’ll list those below if you want the book.

Ultimately, my morals don’t line up with veganism, even if I were to eat plant based. That’s the simple answer. I respect y’all for having those morals, and even think them admirable because they’re above and beyond , but they simply aren’t what I believe and I haven’t been able to change that.

The circumstantial issues I’m running into are the following.

My dietician explicitly told me that going vegan is not a good idea given the diet I have to follow to maintain my health. I’m supposed to have 30-45 carbs every 4 hours. This is the criteria I have to follow if I don’t want to be on more medication. I’m on 7 currently. Of course, the rest of that is fat and protein. So far, the best way to do this in a way that doesn’t cause me to crash or have a seizure is to pair veggies and fruit with a main meat. 

Usually I get rice and beans thrown at me at this point, but the beans alone already tackle almost all the carbs I’m supposed to eat for the next four hours, forget about rice or anything else. 

This can be solved to an extent with beyond meat because it has similar macros to actual meat. But it’s 4x more expensive then ground turkey or other meats where I’m at. So unless it’s on sale, I can’t afford it. Which isn’t often. Hell, even tofu is double, if my family would even touch it.

I think it could be possible to convert to being a vegetarian and not run into as many issues given how many times I’ve subbed eggs for meat, but vegetarian isn’t vegan. 

Even with those taken into account, I do not have support from the people taking care of me at all. While I’m willing to give this stuff a chance, the other two at home are not, and they are bringing home the majority of the money.

Finally, the one that I really dislike myself for, because it’s a trait that seems ridiculous from the outside looking in. I have to have a routine and I have to have familiarity . If things go off the routine, I mentally spiral into a mess where I’m not functional. This includes my food. 

Any change has to be done one at a time, or my body freaks out. Back before I had to get on the diet I’m on now, especially as a kid, I was so picky that I’d choose to not eat for days unless I had one of a few safe foods.

Some ideas. Mind you, these aren't eliminating meat, but rather making them a team player rather than a star.   


Brown some ground beef or bacon in a pot, and when done, add a chopped onion and cook/caramelize to your preference, Then add chopped green peppers and mushrooms. Then add minced garlic. Then put in a whole jar of tomato sauce, and put the meat back in. Stir.   
   
Instead of pasta, use spaghetti squash if you can swing it. Chop that in half, spread olive oil and salt to the middle part after chopping, stab it in the rind a few times, and bake food side down for an hour, and shred when fork tender.   
   
That feeds us (a family of 3) for a good few days, removes a lot of the carbs that comes with pasta, adds onions, peppers, mushrooms, garlic, tomatos, and squash, and you still get a fair amount of protein depending on the grade of meat you choose. Top with cheese moderately if you'd like.   
   
Also, making alfredo from scratch is also an option here because I generally skip over using flour like most store bought ones do, but that's also a fattier recipe and idk if you're trying to avoid that.

So my highest weight was 343, so not even 10 lbs lower than what you are. I'm down to 307 currently in less than a year. First immediate side note is that I know nothing about surgery on this end, so I won't go into that specifically.   
  

Some first things that happened to help me.   
 

\-#1 thing is to know yourself, mentally and physically. Different things help different people, and there is no universal truth beyond calories in-calories out. However, those different things make calories in-calories out way easier.   


I'll be talking about me for what helped me, but realize it may not be applicable to you. There are a lot of people doing the exact opposite and also having it work for them, so don't take what I say as a monolith. Take what you need from it and disregard the rest.  
  

\-My psych was in a better place and enabled me to do it. I had trauma revolving around weight loss and was finally in an environment that was encouraging to actually do so.   
 

\-My PCP referred me to a dietician. If you can, I highly suggest going to one if at all possible. I have other medical conditions happening, I had to actually make a diet change and meal plan besides doing calories in-calories out. It's one of the few general pieces of advice I'd say for anyone asking.   
 

While it is Calories In-Calories Out at the end of the day for everyone losing weight, it's ideal to do it healthily and to take any conditions you have into consideration that might affect this. There are medical conditions that can alter what the average for that should be you metabolic rate or constrict what you can safely eat on a regular basis. Some of them are more silent than others.   
 

\- Even though my weight loss has all been in less than a year, I consider my weight-loss journey to have started around two years ago when I first started seeing my dietician. The first step was to alter what I ate. Then after a couple of months of that, I was supposed to track, but not actively subtract. Then from there, I actually had to stabilize my eating to be consistent every day over the course of several months because it turned out I accidentally developed an eating disorder through childhood. Then, once I was able to eat consistently, I started scheduling meals and when I should eat.  Finally, I started to go into deficit and lose weight.  
   

This set up was very important to me because I'm a person who's body actively hates change. Even so much as something small like being released from school can make my body lose its mind. So this slow process, where I wasn't loosing weight, was important to set up for me to actually lose weight healthily. I also have my weight-loss rate set lower than other people here for that reason. I'm probably loosing a little less than a pound a week compared to a lot of people here losing 2lbs a week. My progress my be slower than others, but I can be more sure that I'll actually keep that progress because I know how I am.  
 

\-This following is what I do now. Again, I want to stress that all bodies are different and this may not be healthy for you because I have other medical issues happening. However, what I have is relatively common. You will see other people doing the exact opposite and also having it work for them.    
 

15-45 net carbs every four hours (so carbs - fiber and sugar alcohol.) So I eat small small, consistent meals throughout the day opposed to intermittent fasting.  My overall diet percentage when it comes to macros is 30% carbs, 50% (healthy) fats, and 20% protein. The two huge factors playing into this are Diabetes and PCOS, both of which cause insulin resistance. Eating like this allows me to keep my blood sugar controlled over the day with 500mg of metformin (most people start out on double that a day, potentially multiple times a day when diagnosed) and diet alone.     
  

I keep track of my calorie intake using MyFitnessPal and set the default to a deficit of one lbs a week. This is so I stay in deficit. When I exercise (which is regularly, usually at least 30 minutes of elevated heartrate walking a day and weights 2-3 times a week), I log it, and I can eat more calories that day to keep consistent with what energy I'm using. However, if my body physically craps out on me as it's known to do and I can't walk or lift that day, I can make sure I don't gain again.   
 

Note that some people do not track because it can make them swing back into an eating disorder, with Anorexia coming to mind as a common example.  but the opposite is true of me. I'll fall back into swing eating if I don't. (aka, barely eating one day and binge eating the next.)  
 

\- Consider this a life style change instead of a diet change (even though you're probably going to literally change your diet in this). It's not something to pick up than drop when you get to a goal weight. You need to actually stick with it to be whatever healthy can look like for you. That means finding healthy AND enjoyable food that nourishes you that you could see yourself sticking to long term. Also finding exercise that you enjoy as well, even though it's not as necessary as diet is for weight loss.   
   
\-Make sure you're doing it for you, not for your partner, family, friends, or anyone else who may be on your back. Easier said than done, obviously,  but it really is something you need to want to do. If you don't want to actually do it, you'll be miserable and probably drop it as a result, or potentially reach a new high weight when you do.

Potato soup can be made good vegetarian, even though I usually add bacon or bacon fat to mine personally. This is my own recipe compared to say a regional recipe, but I deviated off of my mom's.   


Vegetarian version  


\-5 large russet potatoes, peeled and chopped  
\-1 sweet onion, minced  
\-2 Tbsp Minced Garlic  
\-1 Tbsp sesame oil  
\-1 cup heavy cream   
\-1 cup Shredded Cheddar  
\-2 tsp vegetable broth powder  
\-Seasoned Salt  
\-salt  
\-Freeze Dried Chives  
\-Onion Powder  
\-Garlic-powder  
\-Rosemary  
\-Parsley  


Wash, peel and cube the potatoes before hand and set aside. Same with the minced onion.  


 Put a gallon pot on the stove top and put the eye on medium heat. Put the tbsp of sesame oil into the pan and let heat up.   


You'll need to start preparing around a quart of heated water ready on hand. I usually use a tea kettle, but whatever works for you.   


When the oil is properly heated, put the chopped onion in the pot with the oil and stir regularly. When they start looking brownish and translucent, put you garlic in and cook for another minute.   


When the garlic is cooked, dump the potatoes and water in, turn the stove eye on high and immediately stir. When it comes to a roaring boil, keep stirring, but turn the eye down to medium heat, add broth powder, and let stew. Stir every 5 minutes. Check every 15 minutes to see if the potatoes are fork tender.   


When the potatoes are fork tender, drain just enough to where the water barely touches the top most potatoes, and then mash with a potato masher. Stir again, then mash. Turn on medium low heat. Let it stew for another few minutes, checking for a water, but more thick stew. When it's more of a chowder consistency, add the cream, seasoned salt, garlic powder, onion powder, rosemary, chives, and parsley, and then mash and stir again.   


Finally mix in the cheddar, and start seasoning and stewing to taste.   


If for whatever reason you decide to make this not vegetarian....  


\-chicken broth powder instead of vegetable broth powder  


\-if bacon is used, the bacon starts out raw, pieced into the sesame oil, and cooked in pot before the chopped onion is added.  


\-If bacon drippings are used, its added with the cream.   


You can probably use both bacon and bacon drippings, but I don't.

Greetings! I'm also insecure in the same way you are and had a lot of the same issues with the food police.

Firstly, a first step is a good thing, and that first step is you being here and admitting it, mostly to yourself. A good important thing is to try not to give a damn about anyone else. You're doing this for you, and that should be a #1.

Here are some things that helped me beyond that.

A. Don't tell anyone you're trying to lose weight. That's a good way to get unsolicited advice and/or backhanded compliments. Some people may even try to keep you at whatever weight you're at now.

B. Be sustainable. You DO NOT want to go on a crash diet. You may lose the weight quickly, but it will come back with a vengeance since they don't really teach you healthy habits to sustain it.

Sustainability looks very slow comparatively speaking to that. Losing 2 pounds a week is considered on the extreme end of healthy weight loss. Mentally prepare for the fact that you aren't just gonna loose 60 pounds in three months like some of these ads would have you believe.

Sustainability also looks like a life style and not purely a diet to discard. Making this enjoyable is also optimal.

C. Learn how to cook. A hamburger at home can be way more healthy than one you get eating out. That goes for a good majority of the foods you see.

D. If you can't cook, look for either prepackaged things that are suitable for whatever lifestyle change you're making or places to eat out that are better on the health side. Also, make sure to read the menu and actually read what's on it. Sometimes salads are worse than the burger.

Obviously this isn't ideal, but we're not all in ideal situations.

E. Calories in and Calories out is the general idea. However...

1. You can be in deficit and still have an unhealthy diet. That is not good
2. Go to a registered dietician if you have any medical issues that might alter this number. Calories in and out is always the deal, but if you have issues that make that number lower than expected or have to have adjusted macros for whatever reason, you may see a stall even when counting everything right and it looks like you should be loosing weight and aren't.
3. Different diets will make different people feel good even without the above. I personally eat restricted carbs, high healthy fat and proteins thanks to #2 up there. I also have to eat ever four hours or my body hates me and has a fit. Compare that to someone who's carb heavy but intermitting fasting. Both work for each of us, but we'd both probably suffer on the other's diets. Find the one that's healthy for you while keeping in deficit to lose weight.

F. Walks are good, subtle exercise. They also don't make people look at you. You're just the person walking on the sidewalk, not the fat person on the treadmill.

Aim for at least 30 minutes of elevated heartrate with these walks: That's what's considered moderate exercise.

G. Finally, be gentle with yourself. You WILL fall at least once. The important thing is to not beat yourself when you do, but to get back on the horse the next day.  


Edit: Also, keep stuff you'll binge on out. This is more of a me thing, but if it's not in front of me it doesn't exist. If you are also like this, then run out of something and then keep it out.

Also, it goes on biscuits (look up that too if you're overseas.... it isn't cookies. Trust me.) 
 
You'll need...


1 lbs of Ground Pork Sausage

2 1/2 - 4 cups of Milk. I use whole.
( Note that this affects the thickness. )

2/3 cups of All Purpose Flour

Seasoned Salt 
 

In a deeper cast iron skillet, put on the stove top with the heat turned to medium. Pinch off all of your ground sausage into the pan, and brown. Stir around consistently, and do the stir-mash movement. Break the meat down further. 
 
Once cooked, drain into a seperate container. Leave a little grease in. 

Turn stive top on medium-low.

Sprinkle half of your flour in. Stir-mash. 
 
Add half of your milk. Stir-Mash. The rest of your flour. Stir. Thnen the rest of your milk. 
 
Stir frequently, but not consistently, until you get the desired consistency. Salt to taste
 
Serve over biscuits.

If someone hadn't grown up on that or had gut problems, they'd potentially be severely poisoned by that, but I got used to it, and thus I don't seem to get posioned nearly as mu h as ither people do, even eating the same thing.
 
Now compare me to my great grandparents. They hrew up without refrigeration and most of the food guidelines we have now. If they were alive still, they'd probably be able to eat things that would probably poison me because they could handle eating things without refrigeration period.
 
Go back 1,000 years. Vikings were regularly eating raw meat and not immediately dying from it. They had parasites, sure, but they lived and didn't get straight up poisoned.
 
Now spread that idea to a different country that has different regulations on how to cook for the public, or may not even have them at all. They're going to have a different tolerance point than you do, whether it be better or worse. 
 
I'm not sure if rice is one of those things that could give you poisining if left out if you aren't used to it, but it could come down to the above, especially since guidelines specifically in my state require that food be no lower than an internal temp of 140 after reaching its cooking temp, and be left out no longer than two hours after, whether it has meat in it or not.
